terms.meaning: Needs and wants are unlimited, but the resources to meet them are limited. So we must choose.
terms.example: There is not enough land in a city for every use people want.

terms.meaning: Because of scarcity, people, firms and governments must decide how to use limited resources.
The value of the next best thing you give up when you make a choice.
terms.example: If you spend Saturday working, the opportunity cost might be a day skiing.

terms.meaning: A good with no opportunity cost, because using it takes nothing away from anyone else.
terms.example: Air to breathe.

terms.meaning: The resources used to make goods and services: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Natural resources used in production, such as soil, water, forests and minerals.
The physical and mental effort people put into producing goods and services.
Man-made goods used to produce other goods, such as machines, tools and buildings.
Organising the other factors of production and taking risks to start or run a business.
A diagram showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources used fully and efficiently, with given technology.
Some resources, such as workers or machines, are not being used. The economy produces at a point inside its PPC.
Using all resources fully, with no waste. On a PPC, every point on the curve is efficient.
An increase in output from using unemployed resources. On a PPC it is a movement from a point inside the curve towards the curve.
An increase in what the economy is able to produce, from more or better resources or technology. The PPC shifts outward.
Each extra unit of one good costs more and more of the other good, because resources are not equally good at making both. The PPC bows outward.
Each extra unit of one good always costs the same amount of the other good. The PPC is a straight line.
Latin for “all other things being equal”. We change one thing at a time and assume everything else stays the same.
Statements about what is, was or will be. They can be tested with evidence.
terms.example: “A higher bus fare reduced the number of riders.”

terms.meaning: Statements about what ought to be. They are based on value judgments and cannot be tested.
terms.example: “Bus fares should be free.”

terms.meaning: The quantities of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus.
As the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded rises, ceteris paribus. Price and quantity demanded are inversely related.
The amount consumers are willing and able to buy at one particular price.
A change in quantity demanded or supplied caused only by a change in the good’s own price.
The whole curve moves because a non-price determinant changed. More or less is demanded or supplied at every price.
Things other than the good’s own price that shift demand: income, tastes and preferences, future price expectations, prices of related goods, and the number of consumers.
A good whose demand rises when income rises. Its YED is positive.
A good whose demand falls when income rises, because people switch to better alternatives. Its YED is negative.
terms.example: Instant noodles for some consumers.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be used in place of each other. If the price of one rises, demand for the other rises.
terms.example: Tea and coffee.

terms.meaning: Goods used together. If the price of one rises, demand for the other falls.
terms.example: Skis and lift tickets.

terms.meaning: When price falls, a consumer’s real income (buying power) rises, so they can buy more.
When a good’s price falls, it becomes cheaper compared with other goods, so consumers switch towards it.
As a person consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit falls.
The quantities of a good that producers are willing and able to sell at different prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
The amount producers are willing and able to sell at one particular price.

Things other than the good’s own price that shift supply: costs of factors of production, prices of related goods (joint and competitive supply), indirect taxes and subsidies, future price expectations, technology, and the number of firms.
Two goods produced together from the same process, so more of one means more of the other.
terms.example: Beef and leather.

terms.meaning: Two goods that compete for the same resources, so making more of one means making less of the other.
terms.example: A farmer choosing between wheat and canola.

terms.meaning: A tax on spending on goods and services, paid to the government by the seller. It raises firms’ costs, so supply shifts left (up).
A payment from the government to producers for each unit. It lowers firms’ costs, so supply shifts right (down).
The price and quantity where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. There is no pressure for the price to change.
At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied.
At a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.
The way prices change to allocate resources in a market, through signalling, incentive and rationing.
A change in price sends information to buyers and sellers about where resources are wanted.
A change in price motivates buyers and sellers to change what they do, for example producing more when the price rises.
A higher price limits who buys a scarce good to those willing and able to pay it.
The difference between the highest price consumers are willing to pay and the price they do pay. It is the area below the demand curve and above the price.
The difference between the price producers receive and the lowest price they would accept. It is the area above the supply curve and below the price.
Consumer surplus plus producer surplus. It is greatest at the competitive market equilibrium.
Resources are used to make the goods society values most. It happens where marginal benefit equals marginal cost (MB = MC), and community surplus is maximized.
The extra benefit from consuming one more unit. The demand curve shows marginal benefit.
The extra cost of producing one more unit. The supply curve shows marginal cost.
Community surplus that is lost because the market is not at the allocatively efficient quantity.
How much quantity demanded responds to a change in price. PED = %change in quantity demanded ÷ %change in price.
PED is greater than 1 (ignoring the minus sign). Quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price.
PED is between 0 and 1 (ignoring the minus sign). Quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price.
PED equals 1. Quantity demanded changes by the same percentage as price, so total revenue does not change.
PED is infinite. The demand curve is horizontal.
PED is zero. Quantity demanded does not change when price changes. The demand curve is vertical.
The money a firm receives from sales: price × quantity sold (P × Q).
(new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100.
A way to remember what makes PED high or low: Habits, Income share, Necessity, Time, Substitutes.
Number and closeness of substitutes, degree of necessity, proportion of income spent on the good, and time. Many classes also add habits (HINTS).
How much demand responds to a change in income. YED = %change in quantity demanded ÷ %change in income.
Raw materials from farming, fishing, forestry and mining, such as coffee beans, wheat or copper.
How much quantity supplied responds to a change in price. PES = %change in quantity supplied ÷ %change in price.
A legal highest price, set by the government below the equilibrium price. Also called a price ceiling. It causes a shortage.
terms.example: A limit on rents so that tenants pay less.

terms.meaning: A legal lowest price, set by the government above the equilibrium price. Also called a price floor. It causes a surplus.
terms.example: A minimum price for wheat, or a minimum wage.

terms.meaning: A minimum price for labour: the lowest wage firms may legally pay per hour. If it is above the equilibrium wage, it can cause a surplus of labour (unemployment).
terms.example: A law that shop workers must earn at least $20 an hour.

terms.meaning: People or groups affected by a decision or policy, such as consumers, producers, workers and the government.
terms.example: A sugar tax affects drink buyers, drink makers and the government budget.

terms.meaning: How the burden of an indirect tax is shared between consumers and producers. The side with the less elastic curve pays more of the tax.
terms.example: Demand for cigarettes is price inelastic, so smokers pay most of a cigarette tax.

terms.meaning: Meeting the needs of people today without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
terms.example: Catching fish no faster than they can breed keeps the fish stock sustainable.

terms.meaning: Every society must decide what and how much to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.
terms.example: Should a village build houses or boats (what), with machines or by hand (how), and who gets them (for whom)?

terms.meaning: An economic system where private owners and prices answer the basic economic questions, with very little government intervention.
terms.example: Firms make whatever buyers are willing and able to pay for.

terms.meaning: An economic system where the government owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce.
terms.example: A planning office sets how many shoes each factory must make.

terms.meaning: An economic system that uses both markets and government intervention to answer the basic economic questions. Almost all real economies are mixed.
terms.example: Shops are private, but schools and hospitals are paid for by taxes.

terms.meaning: A model of the economy. Money flows from firms to households as incomes, and back to firms as spending. Goods, services and factors of production flow the other way.
terms.example: You earn wages from a shop, then spend them at a café. The café pays its workers, and the money keeps flowing.

terms.meaning: Money that leaves the circular flow of income: savings, taxes and spending on imports.
terms.example: A family puts part of its pay in the bank. That money does not go straight back to firms as spending.

terms.meaning: Money that enters the circular flow of income from outside the household and firm loop: investment, government spending and exports.
terms.example: A firm borrows to build a new factory. That investment adds spending to the economy.

terms.meaning: An opinion about what is good, right or fair. It cannot be proved or disproved with evidence.
terms.example: "Taxes on the rich should rise" contains a value judgement: "should".

terms.meaning: A possible explanation or prediction that can be tested with evidence.
terms.example: Hypothesis: when bus fares fall, more people take the bus.

terms.meaning: Information from observing or measuring the real world, used to test a theory.
terms.example: Counting bus trips before and after a fare cut.

terms.meaning: Showing with evidence that a theory is wrong. A refuted theory is replaced or changed.
terms.example: If bus trips do not rise after a fare cut, the hypothesis is refuted.

terms.meaning: Fairness. What is fair is a value judgement, so people disagree about it.
terms.example: Some people think a fair tax system takes a bigger share from people with higher incomes.

terms.meaning: Everyone having the same, for example the same income or the same opportunities.
terms.example: Equal pay for the same job is an example of equality.

terms.meaning: The idea that markets work best with very little government intervention. Linked to Adam Smith in the 18th century.
terms.example: Letting prices, not the government, decide what firms produce.
